label: Existence and Uniqueness of Moment Maps
notes: Lecture 26 asks two questions about a symplectic action: when does it admit a moment map, and how unique is that map. The answers are cohomological. Existence is blocked in the first de Rham group of the manifold and the first two cohomologies of the acting Lie algebra; uniqueness is governed by the invariants of the coadjoint action.

label: Symplectic vs Hamiltonian Fields
notes: Each generator of the action produces a vector field whose contraction with the form is closed, so the field is symplectic. Being Hamiltonian is stronger: the contraction must be exact. The gap between closed and exact one-forms is exactly the first de Rham cohomology, so that group is the first place an obstruction can live.

label: The First Obstruction in H^1(M)
notes: Walk through the short exact sequence relating Hamiltonian fields, symplectic fields, and the first cohomology of the manifold. A symplectic field is Hamiltonian precisely when its class in that cohomology vanishes. If the whole group is zero, every symplectic field is automatically Hamiltonian and this obstruction disappears.

label: From Action to Comoment Lift
notes: A symplectic action gives a Lie algebra map from g into symplectic vector fields. To build a moment map we lift it to functions, choosing a Hamiltonian for each generator. The lift must be a Lie algebra homomorphism into the Poisson algebra, and assembling it equivariantly across all of g is where the second obstruction appears.

label: Lie Algebra Cohomology H^1 and H^2
notes: Introduce the Chevalley-Eilenberg differential on constant cochains. The first cohomology of g is the annihilator of the commutator ideal, measuring missing brackets. The second cohomology classifies the defect cocycle of an arbitrary lift. These two finite-dimensional groups encode the algebraic side of the existence question.

label: The Defect Cocycle
notes: After picking arbitrary Hamiltonians, the failure to preserve brackets is a constant two-cochain. The Jacobi identity forces it to be a cocycle. If its class in the second Lie algebra cohomology vanishes, a one-cochain correction adjusts the Hamiltonians by constants, repairing the bracket relation without changing any vector field.

label: Existence Theorem
notes: Collect the conditions. A moment map exists when the first de Rham cohomology of the manifold vanishes and the second cohomology of the acting Lie algebra vanishes. The first condition makes each field Hamiltonian; the second makes the choices compatible. Either vanishing alone removes one of the two obstructions.

label: Semisimple Groups Always Work
notes: Whitehead's lemmas say a semisimple Lie algebra has vanishing first and second cohomology with real coefficients. Both obstructions vanish at the algebra level regardless of the manifold, so a symplectic action of a compact semisimple group always admits a moment map. This is the cleanest existence statement in the lecture.

label: The Torus Counterexample
notes: On the two-torus with its standard area form, rotation in the first angle has contraction equal to the second angle one-form. That form is closed but not exact: its period around the second cycle is two pi. So the action is symplectic but not Hamiltonian, showing the de Rham obstruction is genuinely nonzero.

label: Uniqueness up to Invariant Constants
notes: Adding a constant element of the dual algebra to a moment map does not change any Hamiltonian vector field. Equivariance restricts the allowed constants to those fixed by the coadjoint action, equivalently those vanishing on every bracket. So two moment maps for the same action differ by such an invariant constant and nothing more.

label: The Ambiguity Space
notes: The space of moment maps is affine, modeled on the coadjoint-invariant part of the dual algebra, which is the annihilator of the commutator ideal. For semisimple g this is zero, so the moment map is unique. For abelian g it is all of the dual, the maximal ambiguity, matching the abelianization picture.

label: Summary and Dictionary
notes: Summarize the dictionary: first de Rham cohomology separates symplectic from Hamiltonian fields; first and second Lie algebra cohomology control the equivariant lift; the invariant part of the dual algebra measures uniqueness. Compact semisimple groups land in the clean corner with existence and uniqueness both guaranteed.
